text:
Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador,
Court of Appeal

R. v. Devereaux

Date: 1996-12-13

Wayne Gorman, for the Appellant;

Stephen Marshall, for the Respondent.

(1995 No. 125)

December 13, 1996.

[
1
]

Steele, J.A.:

The complainant, one Brian Nolan, was
arrested pursuant to the provisions of the
Detention of Intoxicated Persons
Act
(a provincial statute) and detained at the Lock-up, St. John’s,
overnight. The next morning while awaiting his release, Nolan allegedly used
abusive language and refused to sign a “property release form” until he was
advised of the name of the arresting officer the night before, who purportedly
had made disparaging remarks about his sexual orientation. Having refused to
sign the form, the complainant was restrained and physically placed back in his
cell by the respondent Devereaux, a correctional officer at the Lock-up. Nolan
subsequently signed the property release form and was immediately released. The
respondent was charged with assault but acquitted following a trial in
Provincial Court. The Crown appealed the acquittal to the Supreme Court, Trial
Division; the appeal court judge dismissed the appeal. This appeal by the Crown
is from the decision of the appeal court judge upholding the acquittal by the
trial judge in the Provincial Court and concerns
s. 25
of the
Criminal Code

and
the “peace officer defence”.

Background

[
2
]

Brian Nolan was arrested July 7, 1993, by
members of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary pursuant to the provisions of
the
Detention of Intoxicated Persons Act,
Revised Statutes of
Newfoundland, 1990, c. D-21. He was taken to the City Lock-up in downtown St.
John’s, where the respondent, a correctional officer employed by the
Penitentiary Service, was on duty.

[
3
]

The respondent testified that Nolan was loud,
belligerent, smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and was protesting his
arrest by shouting that he had been arrested because he was a homosexual.

[
4
]

The next morning Nolan was taken out of his cell
to be released. The evidence of the respondent and one Barry Whitty, another
correctional officer present at the time, was to the effect that upon Nolan
leaving his cell he approached the counter and requested the name of the
officers who had arrested him. Whitty told him that the officer was Constable
Larry Hickey but the complainant also wanted the name of the other officer who
had made comments about him being gay. Both Whitty and the respondent testified
that the complainant became aggressive and continued banging his fist on the
counter demanding to know the second officer’s name. At that point the
complainant Nolan was told by Whitty that if he did not sign the form he would
be put back in the cell. According to the respondent’s testimony “at this time,
I went around to the outside of the counter and requested Nolan to sign the
form. I placed my hand on his shoulder and told him that if he didn’t sign the
form, he would have to go back in the cell”.

[
5
]

The version of events related by Whitty and the
respondent Devereaux and that of the complainant differs. The respondent says
he approached Nolan in a non-threatening manner and placed his hand on his
shoulder indicating he should sign the form or he would have to be placed back
in the cell; that Nolan pushed him away, swore at him, and he then applied a
proper restraining hold and escorted him back to the “drunk tank” placing him
on the mattress. According to the respondent’s statement, Nolan was told that
when he “calmed down” and signed the property release form he would be
released.

[
6
]

Nolan alleges that he was viciously punched in
the stomach, choked and kneed in the back while lying on his stomach on the
mattress. An examination by a doctor revealed no evidence of injury.

[
7
]

Following a very short interval in the cell
Nolan agreed to sign the form and upon doing so was immediately released.

[
8
]

Nolan subsequently laid an information alleging
that the respondent Devereaux “… did unlawfully commit an assault upon Brian
Nolan thereby committing an assault punishable on summary conviction, contrary
to
s. 266
(b) of the
Criminal Code of Canada
”.

Trial
Judgment

[
9
]

In the course of his oral judgment the
Provincial Court judge held that the penitentiary operational procedures can
reasonably be interpreted to permit holding an individual until he signed the
appropriate form; that the respondent believed he was acting reasonably and had
reasonable and probable grounds to detain the complainant until he signed the
form; that the respondent had no intent to act illegally and believed he was
following “practices and procedures which he had been directed to follow”; and
that the respondent was not acting illegally in following the directives
relating to the practices of detention and release. The trial judge held that
the Crown had not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt and found the
respondent not guilty.

[
10
]

On appeal to the Trial Division, the appeal
court judge upheld the acquittal and dismissed the appeal.

[
11
]

Respondent’s counsel suggested that the police
detained the complainant Nolan in the morning at the Lock-up, putting him back
in his cell, because he was “causing a nuisance”. I agree with Crown counsel,
and with the trial judge, that Nolan’s refusal to sign the property release
form, Form C-13, was the real reason he was physically taken back to his cell,
and not his alleged antics and abusive behaviour. Undoubtedly, had Nolan signed
the form when first requested, he would have been promptly shown the door, not
the bars from inside a cell.

[
12
]

Section 4 of the
Detention of Intoxicated
Persons Act
authorizes the police to detain a person in an intoxicated
condition and s. 5 concerns his or her release from custody. The following are
the relevant portions of ss. 4 and 5:

“4(1) Where a peace officer finds in a
place to which the public has access a person who is in an intoxicated
condition, he or she may, where that peace officer is of the opinion that the
person may

(a) be a
danger to himself or herself;

(b) be a
danger to others; or

(c) cause a
nuisance,

take that person into custody.

“5(1) Where a person is taken into
custody under section 4, the person having custody of him or her shall release
that person

(a) on his or
her recovering sufficient capacity to remove himself or herself without danger
to himself or herself or others and without causing a nuisance.”

The
Detention of Intoxicated Persons Act,
and
ss. 4 and 5 in particular, do not cover a situation where a detainee eligible
for release refuses to execute a receipt for the return of his property and
valuables.

Prisons
Act And Regulation

[
13
]

The City of St. John’s Lock-up, located off
Water Street, on the ground floor of the Court House building, is an “institution”
of long standing. The Lock-up comes under the jurisdiction of the penitentiary
service, pursuant to the
Prisons Act,
Revised Statutes of Newfoundland,
1990, c. P-21. Section 8 stipulates that:

“The superintendent, the assistant
superintendent and other permanent members of the staff, as defined by
paragraph 2(e), are constituted peace officers and have and may exercise,
within the penitentiary and its precincts and surroundings, the powers possessed
by or given to a member of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary.”

Members of the staff are defined in s. 2(e) of
the
Prisons Act
as follows:

‘“staff includes the superintendent and
assistant superintendent and other commissioned officers and non-commissioned
officers, correctional officers, and other persons employed at the
penitentiary.”

The respondent Devereaux is described as a
correctional officer and by definition he is also a “peace officer”, with
powers of a policeman given to members of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary,
that may be exercised within the penitentiary, its precincts and surroundings.
As we shall see, this authority is relevant when discussing
s. 25
of the
Criminal
Code

respecting legal protection for those involved in the administration
or enforcement of the law as a peace officer, public officer or by virtue of
the office held.

[
14
]

At the trial in Provincial Court, Donald
Saunders testified for the Crown. He stated that he held the position of
Superintendent of Prisons since June, 1990, and was responsible for seven
correctional centers and two lock-ups for the day-to-day operations, and
supervision of staff and inmates. In response to a question from the Crown
prosecutor whether as Superintendent he was responsible and involved in the
making of policy for the release of inmates he replied: “yes, the operational
policy would come under my responsibility”.

[
15
]

Section 9(3) of the
Prisons Act
reads:

“The superintendent may make rules not
inconsistent with this Act respecting routines, procedures and duties to be
carried out by the staff.”

The
Prisons Regulations, 1985
were
published in The Newfoundland Gazette March 8, 1985. Regulations 7(a) and (b)
read:

“7. An officer shall

(a) obey the
lawful instructions of a superior officer;

(b) comply
with the rules respecting routines, procedures and duties made pursuant to
subsection (3) of section 10 of the Act.”

Regulation 8.1(a) provides:

“8.(1) An officer shall not:

a) disobey the
lawful command of an officer who is superior in rank or is in supervisory
capacity over that officer.”

[
16
]

It will be noted that Regulation 7(b) refers to “the
rules respecting routines, procedures and duties made pursuant to subs. (3) of
s. 10 of the Act”. The reference to s. 10 must be an error as s. 10 concerns “offences”.
It is obvious that the reference should have been to s. 9 of the Act as subs.
(3) of s. 9 (quoted above) relates to “routines, procedures and duties to be
carried out by the staff, pursuant to the “rules made by the superintendent”.
This recital of statutory authority brings us to the “Operational Procedures -
Release/Discharge Procedures”, the authority or law on which the respondent
Devereaux relied to physically place Nolan back in his cell when he refused to
sign the property release form. Exhibit D.S. (Donald Saunders) #1 is the “Operational
Procedures - Release/Discharge Procedures No. 6.10 dated April 1, 1982. The
following are the relevant portions of the Operational Procedures:

“Upon the release or discharge of any
inmate held in custody, the
releasing officer shall ensure that the inmate’s
property and
balance of
funds
held in safekeeping during the period
of incarceration
are returned to him
.

“The inmate
shall be required to sign

the personal
property sheet certifying that he has received his property

from the Clothes Room. Also,
he shall be required to sign a receipt for his ‘valuable
property’
and the
releasing officer shall countersign
the property
sheet.

. . . . .

“
The following should be checked prior
to releasing or discharging an inmate
:

(b)
personal
property form
checked
against items received
(checked by
officer-in-charge of Clothes Room).

(c)
money
returned and signed for by inmate
(checked by both the releasing officer
and accounts officer).” (My emphasis added)

It is evident that the Operational Procedures,
and the above passages in particular, do not explicitly cover the course of
action to be followed in the event an individual refuses to sign a receipt for
his property and valuables on release.

[
17
]

(It is immaterial at this point, but some five
months after the incident at the Lockup the Operational Procedures were amended
to the effect that if a detainee refused to sign a receipt for his property and
valuables, he had to be released as scheduled and his property held in trust.
Later, further amendments were made.)

[
18
]

Crown counsel points out that on the assumption
the trial judge concluded that the respondent Devereaux honestly believed he
was acting lawfully in placing Nolan back in his cell, “that such a belief even
if honestly held, cannot constitute a defence as it is a mistake of law”; that
ignorance of the ambit of his authority to apply force is not a valid defence.
No doubt it was the absence of a provision in the statute, in the regulations,
or in the Operational Procedures expressly authorizing the detention of a
detainee at the time of release if he or she refused to sign the release of
property form, that prompted Crown counsel to cite s. 19 of the
Code:

“19. Ignorance of the law by a person who
commits an offence is not an excuse for committing the offence.”

In
R. v. Molis,
1980 CanLII 8 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 356; 33
N.R. 411; 55 C.C.C.(2d) 558, the Supreme Court of Canada considered s. 19. In
Molis

the accused was charged with trafficking in a restricted drug that was not
restricted when he first began manufacturing it, but was subsequently added to
the schedule to the Act. The accused continued to manufacture the drug until
his arrest. At his trial he argued that he did not know it was illegal to
manufacture the drug and that he had exercised due diligence in ascertaining
the state of the law. Appellant’s counsel in
Molis

contended that when
Parliament says ignorance of the law (s. 19) it really means mistake of law,
that is, the wrong interpretation of the law, and that ignorance of the
existence of a relevant penal provision is a defence if an accused has
exercised due diligence in ascertaining the existence of that provision. At p.
563 C.C.C., Lamer, J., writing for the court, stated:

“… Parliament has by the clear and
unequivocal language of s. 19 chosen not to make any distinction between
ignorance of the existence of the law and that as to its meaning, scope or
application …”

[
19
]

Crown counsel says that the respondent Devereaux
cannot rely on his ignorance of the law as a defence and that the trial judge
erred in basing his acquittal on what, in law, is not a valid defence. Further,
he maintains that if the respondent mistakenly believed he was acting lawfully
because his legal authority to apply force extended to detaining someone who
had refused to sign a receipt for his property, that this was a consideration
only on sentencing. Crown counsel submits that the respondent was ignorant of
the law in the sense that he was mistaken as to its interpretation, and by
virtue of s. 19 of the
Code
that mistake, honest as it may have been,
does not constitute a defence.

[
20
]

This particular argument by the prosecution has
merit. I have already pointed out that the relevant statutes, regulations and
the Operational Procedures do not explicitly authorize a correctional officer
to detain an individual if he refuses to sign the appropriate release form. To
that extent it seems the respondent Devereaux misunderstood the Operational
Procedures and s. 19, ignorance of the law is not an excuse, is operative and
deprives the respondent of a defence he may otherwise have had. Nevertheless,
it is not necessary to further analyze s. 19. I have come to the conclusion
that this case falls to be decided under the provisions of
s. 25
of the
Criminal
Code
.
Section 25 of the
Code
concerns persons administering or
enforcing the law who, when carrying out their duties as required or authorized
by law, are legally protected if acting on reasonable grounds and in good
faith, including a situation where the process, (law), is found to be defective.

[
21
]

Subsections (1) and (2) of s. 25 read as
follows:

“25(1) Every one who is required or
authorized by law to do anything in the administration or enforcement of the
law

(a) as a
private person,

(b) as a peace
officer or public officer,

(c) in aid of
a peace officer or public officer, or

(d) by virtue
of his office

is, if he acts on reasonable grounds,
justified in doing what he is required or authorized to do and in using as much
force as is necessary for that purpose.

“(2) Where a person is required or
authorized by law to execute a process or to carry out a sentence, that person
or any person who assists him is, if that person acts in good faith, justified
in executing the process or in carrying out the sentence notwithstanding that
the process or sentence is defective or that it was issued or imposed without
jurisdiction or in excess of jurisdiction.”

[
22
]

Before considering s. 25 of the
Code
and
its application to the case at hand, I wish to make an observation concerning
the milieu in which correctional officers or peace officers carry out their
duties. It would be an exaggeration, in fact not correct, to say that today in
this Province, peace officers belong to a quasi-military organization.
Doubtlessly, the passage of time and the relationship between unions and the
police force has had an impact. Nevertheless, as a generality, police forces
have deep roots in military history. That fact is reflected in the phraseology
appearing in Provincial Statutes, for example, the
Royal Newfoundland
Constabulary Act,
vol. 9, R.S.N. 1990, c. R-16, and the
Prisons Act.
In
reviewing the
Constabulary Act
one sees such terms as: commissioned
officers, noncommissioned officers, force, member, chief, headquarters, patrol
officers, uniforms, etc. In the Prisons
Act
the following expressions
appear: commissioned officers, non-commissioned officers, rank, demotion,
discipline, etc. Also, Regulation 8(1)(a), quoted above, states that an “officer
shall not disobey the lawful command of an officer who is superior in rank …”.
This perspective, a military tradition, reflects the structured background,
training, and police discipline atmosphere in which peace officers,
correctional officers, function and this affinity must be kept in mind when
speaking of the Operational Procedures and in evaluating the comments of Cory,
J., in
R. v. Finta,
1994 CanLII 129 (SCC)
, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 701; 165 N.R. 1; 70 O.A.C. 241; 88
C.C.C.(3d) 417; 112 D.L.R.(4th) 513; 28 C.R.(4th) 265; 20 C.R.R.(2d) 1. I will
refer to
Finta
in some detail shortly.

[
23
]

For our purposes, s. 25, subss. 1 and 2 may be
read as follows: any person required or authorized by law to perform duties in
the administration or enforcement of the law in the capacity of a person
described in paragraphs a, b, c or d, if he or she acts on reasonable grounds,
is justified in performing the duties and may use as much force as is
necessary; and, if a person is required or authorized by law to implement,
enforce or perfect a process and does so in good faith, he or she is justified
(protected) notwithstanding that the method or course of action is legally
flawed or performed without or in excess of jurisdiction. The foregoing is the
measure or test the respondent must ultimately meet.

[
24
]

This much is probably above controversy: that
the respondent Devereaux, as a correctional officer in the penitentiary service
was a peace officer and, what he did at the time in question, the alleged
assault by physically escorting Nolan back to his cell, he did in his capacity
as a peace officer.

[
25
]

Subsection (1) of s. 25 is primarily concerned
with the use of force by those involved in the administration or enforcement of
the law. This subsection puts in issue the individual’s conduct, the use of
force, and whether he acted on reasonable grounds.

[
26
]

The correctional officers in their testimony depicted
Devereaux’s conduct at the counter in the lock-up and on the way to the cell as
being the essence of moderation and restraint. Nolan on the other hand,
portrayed Devereaux’s assault, and the alleged assaults by other correctional
officers, as nothing short of absolute brutality. The trial judge’s finding in
this respect puts the “altercation” in the following context:

“Now I considered it this way. To a
person unfamiliar with the day in and day out routine in the Lockup and of the
interaction between correctional officers and those persons being booked in as
being intoxicated and the upset of many of these people when they are booked in
and when they are being let out, it seems to me to be a common sense matter,
that what might appear to me as a lay person as being a volatile or crisis
situation might, in fact, to people who are involved in this sort of the thing
all of the time and who are trained to deal with these situations, that this
would be no more than a routine incident, and there is certainly no evidence
before me, as I reiterate, as to exactly how much of a commotion was going on.”

[
27
]

The trial judge found as a fact that the
respondent applied a restraining hold on Nolan when physically placing him back
in the cell:

“And there is no dispute that the
accused, Mr. Devereaux, placed a restraining hold on Mr. Nolan and physically
placed him back in the cells. No dispute.”

[
28
]

The trial judge referred to Nolan’s allegations
that he was viciously punched in the stomach, choked and kneed as well as
having been dragged, punched and kicked by police officers at the time of his
arrest. The following statement by the trial judge indicates that he did not
accept the allegations:

“… When he was examined by a doctor
shortly after the Lockup incident, there was no evidence presented, or no
medical evidence, of any visible injuries, and the examination was carried out
at a time proximate to the assaults when such physical assaults as described
would in all likelihood result in some visible manifestation in the form of
scratches or bruises. Mr. Nolan stated emphatically that the assaults took
place, however, there is no evidence before the court to substantiate it.”

[
29
]

The conclusion reached by the trial judge on the
issue of the degree of force used is clearly stated as follows:

“There is no evidence to substantiate
that any more force than was required for that purpose was used by the officer.”

[
30
]

Clearly, the finding by the trial judge is that
the respondent used only as much force as was necessary. I know of no reason to
dispute this finding of fact by the trial judge, the implication being that the
trial judge concluded that the respondent acted reasonably in the
circumstances, using only the degree of force required to return Nolan to his
cell.

[
31
]

Subsection (2) of s. 25 anticipates a situation
where, as here, a peace officer carries out duties he understands are required
or authorized by law, and subsequently discovers that his authority, the law,
is flawed or defective and that he was not “required or authorized by law” to conduct
himself as he did. In such an eventuality the subsection offers refuge to the
extent that his acts will be deemed justified if at the time in question he
acted reasonably and in good faith. The protection offered by subs. (2) of s.
25 is a defence - the defence being that his acts or conduct were “in good
faith”. The justification for his conduct, if the presumed law is defective,
lies in answer to the question of whether he acted reasonably and in good
faith. More will be said shortly about “reasonableness”.

Good
Faith

[
32
]

The term “good faith” in legal parlance is one
of those familiar terms that does not have a precise definition, not quite
self-explanatory, yet is an expression that instantly connotes honesty in a
relationship. In law it is a term that acquires its legal meaning from the
context of the subject in which it appears, both in civil and criminallaw. For
example, in labour law, upon certification of a union there is a duty placed on
all parties to “bargain in good faith”. The expression “bad faith” also has a
prominent place. Labour lawyers describe “good faith” within the framework of
collective bargaining. In the law of defamation, one hears of “fair comment”
and an honest belief in the truth of the facts on which the comment is made;
further, that the comment or opinion must be asserted honestly and in “good
faith”.

[
33
]

Turning to criminal law, the term “good faith”
finds a prominent place in the law of search warrant procedure. James A.
Fontana in his legal text,
The Law of Search and
Seizure in Canada, (3rd
Ed. 1992), at p. 291, discusses the liability and protection of a peace officer
under
s. 25
of the
Criminal Code
.
It was inevitable therefore, that the
Charter
of Rights
and Freedoms,
s. 8 in particular, (having the right to be secure
against unreasonable search or seizure), would soon be at a variance with
s. 25

and law officers engaged in search warrant procedures. R. v. Kokesch,
1990 CanLII 55 (SCC)
, [1990] 3
S.C.R. 3; 121 N.R. 161; [1991] 1 W.W.R. 193; 61 C.C.C.(3d) 207; 1 C.R.(4th) 62;
51 B.C.L.R.(2d) 157; 50 C.R.R. 285, is a good example of the problems that
arise where a search is made without lawful authority and the court has to
decide if the evidence obtained is to be excluded. One of the three broad
categories to be considered in assessing the admissibility of evidence under
s.
24(2)
of the
Charter
is the “seriousness of the violation”. In
Kokesch
,

Sopinka, J., at p. 228 C.C.C. in considering an aspect of the seriousness
of the violation, commented that the manner in which the police conducted
themselves was important and he asked the question: “Was the s. 8 violation
committed in ‘good faith’, or was it ‘flagrant’? Both are terms of art in s.
24(2) cases”. The term “flagrant” was probably borrowed from the statement by
Le Dain, J., in
R. v. Therens,
1985 CanLII 29 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613; 59 N.R. 122; 40
Sask.R. 122; [1985] 4 W.W.R. 286; 18 D.L.R.(4th) 655; 32 M.V.R. 153; 45
C.R.(3d) 97; 18 C.C.C.(3d) 481, at p. 652 S.C.R:

“The relative seriousness of the
constitutional violation has been assessed in the light of whether it was
committed in good faith, or was inadvertent or of a merely technical nature, or
whether it was deliberate, wilful or flagrant.”

[
34
]

We are not concerned with the
Charter

or
whether there was a breach of a
Charter
right. The respondent was
charged with common assault. The point to be made in raising the issue of the
seriousness of a
Charter
breach, is that while good faith (by the
police) is not fully defined, an act committed in “good faith” is conspicuously
set up in opposition to “deliberate, wilful or flagrant” conduct.

[
35
]

The
Canadian Law Dictionary
by John A.
Yogis, Q.C. describes “good faith” by saying that “to act in good faith, one
must act openly, fairly and honestly, …”. If there is one word that delineates
or characterizes the expression “good faith”, it is “honesty”.

[
36
]

To return to the case at hand, subs. (2) of s.
25 of the
Code
provides that a person who is required or authorized by
law to execute a process is, if he acts in good faith, justified in executing
the process notwithstanding that the process is defective or was issued without
or in excess of jurisdiction. The immediate task is to ascertain if the
respondent Devereaux’s actions were in good faith, to be determined from the
evidence -the facts and circumstances of the case.

[
37
]

The question is, therefore, whether the
respondent Devereaux acted in good faith in physically taking Nolan back to his
cell, presumably in the expectation he would soon reassess his plight and,
albeit grudgingly, sign the property release form to gain his liberty. In the
circumstances of this case, “good faith” depends primarily on whether the
respondent held an honest belief he was merely doing his job - performing his
assigned duties - according to orders set down in the Operational Procedures.
In determining if the respondent Devereaux acted in good faith on the night in
question, the most serious question of all is whether he held an honest belief
he was acting legally in detaining Nolan for refusing to sign the appropriate
form.

Was
Respondent’s Conduct Reasonable?

[
38
]

In paraphrasing the Operational Procedures, the
following phrases are accented:

“… releasing officer
shall
ensure
that the inmate’s property … and funds … are returned to him;

“…
shall be required to sign
…
property sheet certifying that he has received his property … he
shall be
required to sign a receipt
for his ‘valuable property’ … releasing officer
shall

countersign …;

“… the following should be checked prior
to releasing or discharging an inmate: personal property form … against items
received, money returned and
signed by inmate
…;”

[
39
]

Under s. 25(2) the emphasis is on the question
of good faith that takes into account an honest belief - an honest belief that
the actions and course of conduct is legal: “required or authorized by law”.
Both subss. (1) and (2) of s. 25 presuppose a reasonableness test or
requirement. Subsection (1) provides in part that the individual in question is
justified in doing what he is required or authorized to do “if he acts on
reasonable grounds”. The acts of the person therefore, must meet the
reasonableness standard. I have already discussed the degree of force aspect.
Subsection (2) is the situation where the legal authority to act, the law,
subsequently turns out to be defective and the justification defence exists
only where “that person acts in good faith”. The honest belief in the legality
of the conduct must also be founded on reasonable grounds.

[
40
]

The trial judge considered the reasonableness of
Devereaux’s actions in detaining Nolan, expressing his opinion this way:

“…. Now these sign out procedures were in
effect for a fairly lengthy period of time. Evidence was presented that this
situation sometimes occurred, and when faced with continued detentions, the
detainee would then sign the release. There was also presented that in such
situations, the correctional officer would contact a superior officer for
direction and advice. I find that the accused’s interpretation of these
directives was reasonable given the written directives contained in the
Operational Procedures relating to discharge and release and the long (held)
policies and practices being followed by the correctional personnel. I find
that the accused believed he was acting justifiably on reasonable and probable
grounds to detain the complainant until he signed or at least until he was able
to get advice from a superior officer. I cannot find any intent on the part of
the accused to act illegally as I have found that he was following practices
and procedures which he had been directed to follow.”

It will be recalled that the Operational
Procedures in effect were dated April 1, 1982, some 11 years prior to the night
in question. Without saying so literally, the trial judge found that Devereaux
acted with the honest belief he was performing a lawful act and that his honest
belief was reasonably held. I am aware of no valid ground to challenge his
conclusion.

[
41
]

It is on the basis of the Operational Procedures
that the respondent says he understood or believed he could not permit Nolan to
leave the Lock-Up unless the proper receipt form was duly signed. Prior to the
night in question the Operational Procedures had been interpreted and were
understood to mean that a detainee or inmate could not be released until he or
she executed the receipt form. The incident involving the complainant Nolan was
not the first occasion that correctional officers had returned an inmate or a
detainee to his cell for refusal to sign the property release form. The
precedent had been set and it was against that background the respondent
recognized the practice and presumed he had full authority to physically return
Nolan to his cell on refusal to sign the form.

[
42
]

Relying on the interpretation given to the
Operational Procedures by correctional officers at the Lock-up, Devereaux
understood and took it for granted he had the authority to detain Nolan when he
refused to sign a receipt for his personal property. It was a reasonable
assumption in the circumstances and a logical basis on which to form an honest
belief he was acting legally. As I read the transcript of the evidence,
Devereaux and the other correctional officers were clearly under the impression
they had no other alternative and, assuredly, to release a detainee who would
not sign an acknowledgement for his valuables would constitute a breach of
their orders.

[
43
]

Devereaux’s honest belief he was authorized by
law to physically detain Nolan was reasonably held and he acted rationally in
the circumstances; he had no reason to doubt he had the authority he purported
to hold. The respondent held an honest belief he was acting legally, in a
manner prescribed by law; a duty he discharged in an acceptable manner. It must
be said therefore, that the respondent acted in good faith, and was justified
in executing the performance of his duties as he perceived them.

[
44
]

There is another aspect to the defence made
possible by s. 25 and it has been alluded to above. It is a circumstance where
the Operational Procedures are of less significance and the emphasis is on the
Superintendent for Prisons and orders from a superior officer. It may be
helpful to again repeat regulations 7 and 8(1)(a) of the
Prison Regulations,
1985:

“7. An
officer shall

(a) obey the
lawful instructions of a superior officer;

(b) comply
with the rules respecting routines, procedures and duties made pursuant to
subsection (3) of section 10 of the Act.

“8(1) An officer shall not:

(a) disobey
the lawful command of an officer who is superior in rank or is in supervisory
capacity over that officer.”

[
45
]

I have already acknowledged that correctional
officers are peace officers, but are not considered as members of the military.
That statement is probably true yet, a military tradition is a relevant
consideration. It may not be feasible to plead the defence of “obedience to
superior orders”, but on reading the
Prison Regulations,
the Operational
Procedures, and recognizing the status and role of the Superintendent of
Prisons, such a prospect is not absurd. It would seem that had there been no
Operational Procedures, the likelihood would be that the episode that occurred
would still have happened, and the reason is the constant stewardship and
involvement of the Superintendent.

[
46
]

It is important to remember that this case is
dissimilar in at least one respect to cases cited where the problem arose from
the exercise of authority or power derived from the common law or generally
from authority vested in the accused as a peace officer. (See
Eccles v.
Bourque et al.,
1974 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739; 3 N.R. 259; 19 C.C.C.(2d) 129;
R.
v. Brennan
(1989),
1989 CanLII 7169 (ON CA)
, 36 O.A.C. 218; 52 C.C.C.(3d) 366 (C.A.);
R. v.
Vassallo
(1983),
1983 CanLII 2848 (PE SCAD)
, 43 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 305; 127 A.P.R. 305;
1983 CanLII 3561 (PE SCAD)
, 8 C.C.C.(3d)
427 (P.E.I.C.A.); and
Interception of Private Communications Reference,
1984 CanLII 31 (SCC)
, [1984]
2 S.C.R. 697; 56 N.R. 43; 58 A.R. 39; 15 C.C.C.(3d) 466). In this case the
respondent’s actions were not the result of the exercise of his judgment or
discretion in a situation where he believed his authority was basic to his
position as a peace officer or inherent in his office as a correctional
officer. Once it was obvious that Nolan would not sign the property release
form, Devereaux’s course of action was mandatory: return the detainee to his
cell - hopefully temporarily. If the problem persisted, and that did not happen
here, the  Superintendent’s office was contacted for advice and directions.
Certainly, good intentions and an honest belief that his actions were lawful
were present, but as far as the respondent Devereaux was concerned, there was
no misunderstanding the scope of his authority: for 11 years or so it had been
the policy and practice, upon the order of the Superintendent, to detain
persons who refused to sign a receipt for their property at the time of their
release.

[
47
]

The policy and practice of returning a detainee
to his cell in the event he refused to sign a receipt for his property existed
at least from April 1, 1982, when the Operational Procedures (Exhibit D.S. #1)
came into force. Present with the written Operational Procedures in 1993 was
the longstanding endorsement and enforcement of the policy that found
expression from time to time, in difficult circumstances, in verbal directions
from the Superintendent. It is apparent that the Operational Procedures were
misread, nevertheless, Devereaux and other correctional officers were under the
constant supervision of the Superintendent for Prisons who ultimately was
responsible. As Superintendent Saunders testified he was “responsible for the
day to day operations, and supervision of staff and inmates”. Devereaux was
obliged to follow the Operational Procedures, but in addition he was subject to
verbal instructions and orders. The Operational Procedures of 1982 may have
been deficient and misunderstood by Devereaux yet, the Operational Procedures
aside, he was always subjugated to the verbal directions and orders of his
superior, the Superintendent. This analysis of
s. 25
of the
Criminal Code

finds
support in
R. v. Finta
,
supra.

[
48
]

In
Finta
,
the accused, Imre Finta, was
born in Hungary, now a part of Romania. He studied law and in 1935 enrolled in
the military academy and in 1939 was commissioned as an officer in the Royal
Hungarian Gendarmerie described as an armed paramilitary police force. In 1944
he became a commander of the investigative sub-division. At that time Hungary
was occupied by the German army. The Hungarian police and the Gendarmerie came
under the direct command of the German S.S. The charges against Finta involved
the allegation that he was in charge of the “de-jewification” that was
authorized by the so- called “Baky Order” that called for the isolation,
complete expropriation, concentration camps and eventual deportation of all
Hungarian Jews. It was referred to as the “final solution” to the “Jewish
problem”.
R. v. Finta

concerned war crimes and crimes against humanity,
proof of offences arising from detention, robbery, and deportation to
concentration camps, etc. The Supreme Court, amongst many other issues,
considered the defence of a police officer following a lawful order, and
whether the “peace officer defence” was available and the nature of that
defence. The Supreme Court was obliged therefore, to consider s. 25 of the
Code

and the so-called police/peace officer defence.

[
49
]

At p. 825 S.C.R., of
Finta,
Cory, J.,
made the following statement in introducing s. 25:

“Section 25 of the
Code
provides
the accused with a justification for the use of as much force as is necessary
to do anything in the administration or enforcement of the law, notwithstanding
that the law is defective.”

At p. 826 S.C.R., Justice Cory makes the
following comment concerning the peace officer defence provided by s. 25 of the

Code:

“The peace officer defence, set out
above, is similar to the defence of obedience to military orders. The latter
defence is recognized by most systems of criminal law. (See, e.g., L.C. Green,
Superior
Orders and Command Responsibility
(1989), 27 Can. Y.B. Intl L. 167.) It is
based on the well-recognized principle that in both the armed force and police
forces commands from superior officers must be obeyed. It follows that it is
not fair to punish members of the military or police officers for obeying and
carrying out orders unless the orders were manifestly unlawful …”

[
50
]

The appellant argued in
Finta

that the
effect of s. 7(3.74), which limits the accused’s right to plead obedience to de
facto law, is to preclude the use of the police officer defence under
s. 25
of
the
Criminal Code
.
The thrust of that argument was that s. 25(2) was
contrary to the purpose of
s. 7(3.74)
. That aspect of
Finta
is of little
interest and need not be explained, but in the course of his analysis Justice
Cory made the following statement at p. 842 S.C.R. concerning
s. 25
:

“… The purpose of s. 25(2) is to provide
legal protection to a peace officer, who, acting in good faith and on a
reasonable belief that his or her actions are justified by law, later finds out
that those actions were not authorized because the law was found to be
defective.

“Section 25 is akin to the defence of
mistake of fact. Unless, the law is manifestly illegal, the police officer must
obey and implement that law. Police officers cannot be expected to undertake a
comprehensive legal analysis of every order or law that they are charged with
enforcing before taking action. Therefore, if it turns out that they have
followed an illegal order they may plead the peace officer defence just as the
military officer may properly put forward the defence of obedience to superior
orders under certain limited conditions. The qualification is that the military
officer must act in good faith and must have reasonable grounds for believing
that the actions taken were justified. An officer acting pursuant to a
manifestly unlawful order or law would not be able to defend his or her actions
on the grounds they were justified under
s. 25
of the
Criminal Code
.”

[
51
]

Also at p. 842 S.C.R., Justice Cory referred to
the trial judge’s instructions to the jury observing that:

“… The peace officer defence would be
available only if the law or orders were not manifestly illegal and if the
accused honestly, and on reasonable grounds, believed his actions to be
justified. For example, the following instructions given to the jury were, in
my view, entirely appropriate.

‘So it is very
important to judge a policeman or soldier, anyone subject to military
discipline with the test of whether they acted honestly and reasonably in all
the circumstances at that time and in that place.

‘These defences are limited. They depend
on honesty, they depend on reasonable conduct, they depend on not using
excessive force. They aren’t a licence to commit a crime. They aren’t a licence
if some government or some deputy minister or some under secretary of state
goes off the rails and tells the policeman or solider to do something that is
clearly illegal. These defences are no licence to commit obvious crimes in the
name of the government.’”

[
52
]

With respect to Cory, J.’s, analysis of
s. 25
,
at p. 845 S.C.R., he again quotes in part the trial judge’s instructions to the
jury with approval:

“He was also correct in instructing the
jury that when the order or law is not manifestly unlawful and the peace
officer or solider acts on reasonable grounds, he is justified in using as much
force as is required for the purpose even if it is later discovered that the
law was defective. He properly told the jury that ‘[i]f the peace officer or
solider honestly believes the law or order is lawful domestically, he acts on
reasonable grounds at the time, he has a right to be wrong even if it turns out
later he was, in fact, wrong’. In my view, this is a correct instruction on the
defence of mistake of fact in combination with the peace officer and military
orders defences. Mistake of fact is applicable only in circumstances where the
order (in the case of the superior orders defence) or law (in the case of the
peace officer defence) is not manifestly unlawful.”

[
53
]

At p. 834 S.C.R., Justice Cory attributes the
following meaning to the term “manifestly unlawful”:

“… When is an order from a superior
manifestly unlawful? It must be one that offends the conscience of every
reasonable, right-thinking person; it must be an order which is obviously and
flagrantly wrong. The order cannot be in a grey area or be merely questionable;
rather it must patently and obviously be wrong. For example the order of King
Herod to kill babies under two years of age would offend and shock the conscience
of the most hardened soldier …”

Conduct to be manifestly unlawful, in the
context of s. 25 of the
Code
and the peace officer defence, must border
on criminality.

[
54
]

In
Finta
,
much is said about the state of
affairs where the order or law is, or is not, “manifestly unlawful”. The
Supreme Court makes it clear that a peace officer acting pursuant to a
manifestly unlawful order or law, cannot defend his actions on the grounds they
were justified under s. 25 of the
Code.
A peace officer, executing a
process or carrying out duties under laws or orders manifestly illegal, can
hardly be heard to say he was acting in good faith and therefore justified. A
manifestly unlawful act could on no account withstand a reasonableness
assessment. The misconception and actions by Devereaux over the Operational
Procedures and their enforcement, scarcely engendered the evil and oppression
of a magnitude described or contemplated in
Finta
.
Simply put, this is
not a case where a correctional officer acted in a “manifestly illegal” manner.
The Operational Procedures and Devereaux’s conduct were not, from any
perspective, so manifestly illegal that he be disentitled to a defence
permissible under s. 25 of the
Code.
To be denied the “peace officer
defence” the conduct or act would have to be so patently illegal that a plea of
acting in good faith would have absolutely no plausibility whatsoever, making
no sense at all. My reading of s. 25 is that the defence or defences accorded
by that section, are available under the very situation that occurred here,
namely, one that may fairly be characterized as nothing more than an innocent -
honest - misunderstanding by a correctional officer in the carrying out of his
duties prescribed by the Superintendent of Prisons.

[
55
]

The Provincial Court judge did not expressly say
the respondent had an honest belief he was acting legally, but unmistakably
that was his conclusion. Also, Crown counsel in discussing s. 19 of the
Code

-Ignorance of the Law is not an excuse -concedes the likelihood that
although the respondent made a mistake of law, he may well have honestly
believed he was acting lawfully. It may be thought therefore, that it is
unnecessary for me to dwell at length, as perhaps I have, on the meaning of “good
faith” and whether the respondent acted in good faith. As far as I can
determine, both in the Provincial Court and before the appeal court judge, s.
25 of the
Code
was not mentioned. It was necessary therefore, to discuss
in some detail the evidence and the concepts of honest belief and good faith as
they apply to s. 25.

[
56
]

For these reasons I would dismiss the appeal and
confirm the order of the Provincial Court judge dismissing the charge.

Appeal dismissed.
